newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-VW wants court ruling on EU subsidies.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-VW wants court ruling on EU subsidies.

text.p: German carmaker Volkswagen AG said on Friday it has filed a complaint with the European Court of Appeals seeking a decision on its bitter row over subsidies with the European Commission.
VW said the complaint was independent of the temporary deal reached last week that defused the troubles between Germany and the Commission as well as with the Wolfsburg-based carmaker.
"This one action is independent of the other," a VW spokesman said. "We have said we were right in receiving the subsidies and we want the court to clarify what is right."

VW and Brussels have been battling one another since the Commission in June cleared only 540 million ($357 million) of 780 million marks in aid received from the German government and the state of Saxony for projects at VW's plants in the east German cities of Mosel and Chemnitz.

The powerful carmaker countered by threatening to end its investment in the region, plagued by high unemployment, and Saxony defied the Brussels ruling by giving VW about 91 million marks of the controversial subsidies.

Last week's face-saving compromise calls for VW to keep the disputed funds despite the original objections. In return, Bonn has pledged to block an equivalent amount of federal aid that has been authorised by the Commission but not yet paid to VW.

VW's filing of a complaint followed that of Bonn saying on Thursday it would file one before Monday's deadline. The European Commission has also said it would file its own complaint on the saga with the court.

The state of Saxony has already filed a complaint, saying the refusal to grant subsidies would put more than 20,000 jobs in the region -- an economic powerhouse area before World War Two -- in jeopardy.

Talks between Bonn and Brussels over the row will continue, but German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Thursday that Germany would withdraw its complaint if a mutually agreeable solution was found.
If the deal does not hold, the issue would then move to the courts through the suits that have been filed.

The VW spokesman said the carmaker also wanted a "concrete ruling" on interpreting the controversial European Union laws, a case that parties involved have said could take at least two years to be finally settled.
The European Court of First Instance, the EU's lower court, will have to take up the case and decide on the substance of the allegations.
At the centre of Saxony's defence is a contested provision in the EU treaty that allows for subisides to be paid to areas of former East Germany.

The treaty calls for the payments to "compensate for the economic disadvantages" caused by the separation of East and West Germany after World War Two and for the region's rebuilding since unification in 1990.

The European Commission has countered by saying the VW subsidies should be viewed under Commission laws regarding funds for the European car industry, which has been hurt by overcapacity. ($1=1.5126 Mark)
